newsitem.title: MALTA: Malta exchange seeks new listings, including funds.
newsitem.headline: Malta exchange seeks new listings, including funds.

text.p: Malta's stock exchange, with just five listed companies, is launching a triple project to increase its listings, attract collective investment schemes, and promote itself as a regional bourse.

The exchange, set up in 1992, may soon have a sixth company because Suncrest Hotels has announced plans to join. It is talking to another seven firms, chairman Frederick Mifsud Bonnici told Reuters on Thursday.

He sees more listings with a broader range as essential to bring more vitality to the exchange, dominated by financial concerns -- three banks and an insurance company, with the fifth firm being the private brewery and drinks manufacturer, Simons Farsons Cisk.

"Over the past six months we have been dealing with eight companies, a number in the tourist sector which could add a new dimension to the exchange," he said. Others were in services and manufacturing.
"We believe a wider range would produce more investment rather than a switching of investment," he said, adding there was not much scope for buying and selling at present.

Growth of the exchange has been slow, which Bonnici attributes to a "culture" gap. Maltese prefer to save money rather than invest, he said, while businesses were normally family run and conservative.

"People have two main fears, losing control (of their firm) and having to be accountable. But under changes in company law and especially if we go into the European Union they will have to disclose more anyway," he said in an interview.
To tackle this reluctance the exchange has just completed a booklet on "Going Public - Seeking a Listing" - which will go out to family-run businesses.

The exchange needed more privatisation. Prime Minister Eddie Fenech Adami had referred to Air Malta and the Gozo Channel line which operates the ferry service with the sister island of Gozo, as possible targets during campaigning. "All privatisations so far have proved very successful in a very short period ofe," he said, adding: "It looks as though the government might be embarking on a more aggressive approach to privatisations."
All primary issues had been oversubscribed - 12 to 15 times - and Maltese subscribers had risen from 8,000 when the exchange opened to 80,000 now, including 45,000 individuals.

Trading at the once weekly session had also risen, from an average 60 deals to over 100. At the last session on Wednesday 93 deals were completed, 69 in equities and 24 in fixed income securities. Turnover reached just over Lm263,000 ($725,880).
But trading volumes are down, this year so far standing at 19 million against 28 million for the whole of last year.

"There are two pressing points. Further privatisation and accession to Europe. This is going to force our companies if they want to survive competition to invest in new equipment and bring their standards up to scratch, which will need finance.
"And with banks having to comply with the large exposure directives, bank finance will not be as easily available... their only alternative will be to tap the public for funds," Bonnici said.

"We are also trying to develop Malta for listing of collective investment schemes. We see this as a niche in the market and have just completed our rules for this, which will not be 'flags of convenience'."
Only one scheme, La Valette Funds SICAV, with two sub funds, has so far been registered, last year.

With electronic trading fully introduced this year another possible area of expansion was secondary listings. "We are talking to at least 10 groups about this, mainly in Britain but also Switzerland, France and Germany," he said.
Bonnici added that if Middle East peace went the right way, Malta had the potential to become a regional centre.

It had received inquiries from the United Arab Emirates and from Indian and Pakistani companies with operations in the Middle East, and from Israel. He added however that since recent violence in the area nothing further had been heard.
